title: Karnataka Formally Lifts Its Hijab Ban — and Reopens India's Most Polarising Education Debate
excerpt: The Congress government's May 13 order allows hijabs, sacred threads and rudraksha in classrooms, ending a four-year standoff that kept Muslim girls out of schools and split the Supreme Court down the middle.
body:
The notification, when it finally came on May 13, was deliberately dry: Government Order No. ED 22 HCM 2026, citing the Karnataka Education Act of 1983 and the Karnataka Educational Institutions Rules of 1995. But the administrative prose belied the emotional charge. Four years after the BJP government in Bengaluru banned hijabs in classrooms — setting off protests that shuttered schools, polarised communities and produced a split Supreme Court verdict — the Congress government of Chief Minister Siddaramaiah has formally reversed course.

## What the New Order Actually Says

Students may now wear "limited traditional and practice-based symbols" alongside their prescribed uniforms in government schools, aided institutions and private colleges under the state's School Education Department. The list is deliberately ecumenical: hijab, sacred thread (*janeu*), rudraksha, shivadhara and sharavastra are all explicitly permitted.

The order comes with guardrails. Uniforms remain compulsory. The permitted symbols are supplementary items that must not interfere with "discipline, safety, cleanliness or identification." No student may be denied entry for wearing — or refusing to wear — any of them. Institutions have been instructed to implement the policy "in accordance with constitutional principles including equality, dignity, fraternity, secularism, scientific temper, rationality and the right to education."

## The Trigger That Forced the Government's Hand

The Congress government had been in power for three years without touching the ban, even as its rhetoric promised reversal. What changed was the Karnataka Common Entrance Test on May 1. Several students were reportedly asked to remove hijabs and sacred threads before entering examination halls — during a high-stakes entrance exam. Health Minister Dinesh Gundu Rao called the incident "inhuman." School Education Minister Madhu Bangarappa announced the revised order at a press conference alongside Rao and Shivajinagar MLA Rizwan Arshad.

## A Brief History of a Long Standoff

The confrontation dates to December 2021, when Muslim students at a government pre-university college in Udupi were prevented from attending classes while wearing hijabs. Counter-protests erupted, with some Hindu students donning saffron shawls in solidarity with the ban. Schools closed temporarily. In March 2022, the Karnataka High Court upheld the ban, ruling that hijab was "not an essential religious practice in Islam." The matter reached the Supreme Court, which delivered a rare split verdict — one justice upheld the ban while the other struck it down — leaving the High Court order in place.

The practical impact was devastating. Muslim women reported being turned away from classrooms, barred from examinations and subjected to what many described as systematic humiliation. Dropout rates among Muslim girls in Karnataka reportedly rose, though comprehensive data remains contested. Several students filed complaints with the National Human Rights Commission, alleging violations of their fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19 and 25 of the Constitution.

## The BJP Response

The opposition has been swift and predictable. BJP leaders have accused the Congress government of "appeasement politics" and "selective secularism," arguing that the original ban was necessary to maintain equality and public order in educational settings. Former Chief Minister Basavaraj Bommai called the reversal "a vote-bank decision that will divide classrooms." The party has signalled it will challenge the order if it returns to power.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRI families with roots in Karnataka — and for the broader Indian Muslim diaspora — the reversal carries weight that extends well beyond dress codes. Many families abroad had watched the original ban with alarm, seeing it as a test case for religious freedom in Indian public institutions. Parents who had considered pulling daughters out of Indian educational pathways now face a cautious recalibration.

But the fragility of the change is the point. The Supreme Court's split verdict means there is no settled constitutional precedent. A change in government could reverse the reversal. And the BJP's framing of the issue as secularism-versus-appeasement ensures it will remain a live wire in Karnataka's electoral politics.

The Congress government has, for now, chosen to frame the policy as inclusive rather than religious — permitting all faith-based symbols, not just the hijab. Whether that framing holds under political pressure will determine whether this is a durable policy shift or another chapter in a cycle that has already cost a generation of students years of disruption.
